**Answer: No, it is not true.** The weak-* limit of continuous functions need not be continuous.

---

## Counterexample

Take $[a,b]=[0,1]$. Define the discontinuous function
$$f(x)=\mathbf{1}_{[0,\,1/2]}(x)=\begin{cases}1,&0\le x\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt]0,&\tfrac12<x\le 1.\end{cases}$$
This $f$ belongs to $L^\infty([0,1])$ but is **not** continuous at $x=\tfrac12$.

For each $n\ge 3$ define a continuous "ramp" approximation $f_n:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ by
$$
f_n(x)=
\begin{cases}
1, & 0\le x\le \tfrac12-\tfrac1n,\\[4pt]
\text{linear}, & \tfrac12-\tfrac1n\le x\le \tfrac12+\tfrac1n,\\[4pt]
0, & \tfrac12+\tfrac1n\le x\le 1,
\end{cases}
$$
where "linear" means $f_n$ decreases linearly from $1$ to $0$ on $[\tfrac12-\tfrac1n,\tfrac12+\tfrac1n]$. Each $f_n$ is continuous on $[0,1]$, and $0\le f_n\le 1$.

## Verification of weak-* convergence

Recall that $L^\infty([0,1])\cong (L^1([0,1]))^*$, and weak-* convergence $f_n\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} f$ means
$$\int_0^1 f_n(x)\,g(x)\,dx \;\longrightarrow\; \int_0^1 f(x)\,g(x)\,dx \qquad\text{for every } g\in L^1([0,1]).$$

**Pointwise convergence a.e.** For every $x\neq \tfrac12$ we have $f_n(x)\to f(x)$:
- if $x<\tfrac12$, then for all large $n$, $x\le \tfrac12-\tfrac1n$, so $f_n(x)=1=f(x)$;
- if $x>\tfrac12$, then for all large $n$, $x\ge \tfrac12+\tfrac1n$, so $f_n(x)=0=f(x)$.

The only exceptional point is $x=\tfrac12$, a single point, hence a null set. Thus $f_n\to f$ a.e.

**Uniform boundedness.** $|f_n(x)|\le 1$ for all $n$ and all $x$.

**Dominated convergence.** For any $g\in L^1([0,1])$, the integrands $f_n\,g$ satisfy $|f_n g|\le |g|$ with $|g|\in L^1$, and $f_n g\to f g$ a.e. By the Dominated Convergence Theorem,
$$\int_0^1 f_n\,g \;\longrightarrow\; \int_0^1 f\,g.$$

Since this holds for every $g\in L^1([0,1])$, we have $f_n\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup} f$ in $L^\infty([0,1])$.

## Conclusion

We have produced a sequence $(f_n)$ of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ converging weak-* to $f=\mathbf{1}_{[0,1/2]}\in L^\infty([0,1])$, and $f$ is discontinuous. Therefore the weak-* limit of continuous functions **need not be continuous**.
